entry.name: Subjectless Participial Supplement
entry.pattern: nonfinite supplement[V-ing or V-en + dependents] anchored to main clause

1.definition: Adds a circumstance whose understood subject is normally recovered from the anchor.

examples.form: [Hearing footsteps], Jo switched off the light.
Lee shut the door, [startled by the noise].
examples.note: Constructed comparison. The past-participial supplement takes Lee as its understood subject.

projection.target: Jo is the ordinary understood hearer. A separate overt subject would instead support an absolute supplement, while some fixed discourse adjuncts use contextual subjects.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Extra -ing and -ed phrases beside a sentence
curious.summary: A phrase starting with an -ing or -ed verb can add a circumstance to a sentence, with its doer understood from the main clause.
curious.body: In Hearing footsteps, Jo switched off the light, the phrase hearing footsteps adds a circumstance but doesn't say who heard. We understand that it was Jo. In Lee shut the door, startled by the noise, the -ed phrase is understood to be about Lee. The doer is normally taken from the main part of the sentence. If the added phrase has its own subject, it's a different pattern, which this dictionary calls an absolute supplement. Some fixed phrases get their understood subject from the situation instead.

examples.text: [Hearing footsteps], Jo switched off the light.
Lee shut the door, [startled by the noise].

curious.try: Say Hearing footsteps, Jo switched off the light. Who heard the footsteps? Where does the sentence tell you?

teacher.summary: Explains -ing and -ed phrases added to a main clause, and how their understood subject is recovered.
teacher.explain: A subjectless participial supplement is a nonfinite phrase (V-ing or V-en plus dependents) anchored to a main clause. It adds a circumstance, and its understood subject is normally recovered from the anchor: Jo is the hearer in the first example, and Lee is the startled one in the second. A separate overt subject would support an absolute supplement instead. Some fixed discourse adjuncts use contextual subjects. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: Participial phrase is the traditional name. This dictionary calls the pattern a supplement because it's added to the clause and not required by it.

examples.text: [Hearing footsteps], Jo switched off the light.
Lee shut the door, [startled by the noise].

contrasts.text: [Hearing footsteps], Jo switched off the light.
contrasts.note: The understood hearer is Jo, recovered from the main clause.

contrasts.text: [Jo having left], Lee switched off the light.
contrasts.note: A separate overt subject supports an absolute supplement instead.

watch_for: A learner might look for the understood subject inside the phrase, when it is recovered from the main clause.
A learner might expect the subject of startled by the noise to be the door, when this dictionary takes it to be Lee.
teacher.activity: Students underline the participial phrase in each of several sentences and circle who or what it is understood to be about. They then say how they know.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Subjectless Participial Supplement." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/participial-clause-supplement-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).
